public_page_goal: Interactive Markdown lecture notes for MAE598/494 Design Optimization: constrained optimization part 1, covering KKT conditions, constraint qualifications, derivation via reduced gradients, and sensitivity of Lagrange multipliers.
notation: Problem (P): min f(x) s.t. g(x) <= 0 (g: R^n -> R^p), h(x) = 0 (h: R^n -> R^m). Gradients are row vectors; mu (inequality) and lambda (equality) are Lagrange multipliers; L = f + mu^T g + lambda^T h.
slide_outline: KKT point: stationarity, primal feasibility, dual feasibility (mu >= 0), complementary slackness (mu_i g_i = 0).
Geometric interpretation: force balance between -grad f and constraint reaction forces; walls push but never pull.
Active sets: strongly active (g_i = 0, mu_i > 0), weakly active (g_i = 0, mu_i = 0), inactive (g_i < 0).
First-order necessary conditions under a constraint qualification; second-order sufficient conditions on critical directions.
LICQ on all active constraints; Slater's condition for convex problems; KKT is sufficient for convex problems.
Counterexample: min -x1 s.t. x2 <= (1-x1)^3, x2 >= 0 has a solution that is not a KKT point because LICQ fails.
Equality-only derivation: split x = [d; s], implicit function theorem, reduced gradient df/dd.
Lagrange multiplier as adjoint: lambda^T = -(df/ds)(dh/ds)^{-1}; second-order condition via w^T Hess_x L w on the tangent space.
Inequality constraints: treat active constraints as equalities; proof of mu >= 0 using LICQ.
Sensitivity: change in optimal f is approximately -lambda^T dh - mu^T dg; multipliers are shadow prices; envelope theorem dF/dtheta = dL/dtheta.

Exercises: box-constrained quadratic, PCA, linear equality constraints, discrete-time Pontryagin principle, linear and nonlinear PDE-constrained design (adjoint), neural network training (backpropagation), water-filling, manufacturing shadow prices, nearest point on a parabola.
answering_rules: Answer as a concise teaching assistant for an optimization class.
Use the supplied lecture notes first. If context is insufficient, say what is missing.
Prefer equations and small examples over vague descriptions.
The numbered exercises are assigned work: give hints, point to the relevant section, and check the student's reasoning rather than giving full solutions.
Use LaTeX delimiters for math so MathJax can render the answer.
